experiment: closed-loop repair, A/B on fix_plan detail

arms.A: control: the gate prints only the machine code of what failed
arms.B: treatment: the gate prints code, severity, detail, evidence (coordinates) and a fix instruction

design.note: one sample per defect class; each arm edited an independent copy

results.notes: diagnosed by reading the entity table; rebuilt geometry at the scale implied by the surviving dimension text

conclusion: No difference. Both arms repaired every sample on the first attempt.
why: The control arm could read the DXF itself. Every A agent opened the file with ezdxf, inspected the entity table and located the defect without the gate's evidence. Once a model can read the artefact, a fix instruction is redundant information.

The six defects are all locally visible in the entity table: a 3-vertex polyline, a layer attribute, a paper size, a missing INSERT, a collapsed bbox. None required the topology or alias reasoning that would be hard to reproduce by hand.
Repair attempts were unlimited in tool use and cheap; a model that can script ezdxf will find a 3-vertex polyline in one pass.
what_this_does_not_show: It does not show that fix_plan is useless. It shows that this experiment design cannot measure its value: the control arm had the same information by a longer route.
suggested_next: Deny the control arm file reads (give it only the code) so the information gap is real. That measures whether the code alone is actionable.
Raise drawing complexity to hundreds of entities so locating a dangling end by inspection costs many more steps than reading a coordinate.
Measure cost as well as success: tool calls, tokens, wall time. The B agents were visibly more direct even when both succeeded.
Use defects that are not locally visible, for example an outline that is topologically open only after layer filtering, or a dimension whose override disagrees by 0.3%.
